utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, please could you call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is case number IT-99-36-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I welcome you all to this second part of the Pre-Trial Conference. I particularly welcome you, Mr. de Roux, for being present today. I think your presence is particularly needed at this point in time because you will complement the whole picture before we bring it to an end prior to the commencement of the trial. And before I proceed, I would like to know from each one of the accused whether they are hearing me in a language that they can understand. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, can you hear me in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can proceed from that. Appearances, please, on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, together with Andrew Cayley, senior trial attorney, who appears today before Your Honour, so that Your Honour has the full senior complement of the Prosecution, and assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the side of the Defence for General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Xavier de Roux, from the bar of Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Michel Pitron, attorney at the Paris bar, assisted by Mrs. Natasha Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I'm here on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin, and the other person here with me is an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you will recall that at the last Pre-Trial or the first part of the Pre-Trial Conference was held rather recently, last month, on the 10th of December, to be precise, in preparation of the -- for the trial which has been scheduled for the 21st of January. You will also recall that on that occasion, we did not conclude our travail, and we agreed to adjourn to today to deal with all that remains to be dealt with prior to the commencement of the trial. It's almost needless on my part to remind you that basically, unless there is really the need for an extra session, this is the last opportunity that we have to coordinate all our efforts and sort out all the remaining problems before the start of the trial. So my intention is to, like last time, appeal for your consideration, patience, and also cooperation so that we try and conclude what we need -- what needs to be concluded today, within the shortest possible time. I also realise that the last hearing took us four hours, which was long, but it was also needed, anyway, because it gave me the opportunity to get to know you better, and also sort of prepare a platform which was good enough for both sides and the Court, and the Tribunal, to be able to cooperate and go ahead with the trial. May I take the initiative and introduce certain -- some information, give you some information about motions, in particular, those which are outstanding, those which have been very recently decided, and those which will be decided very soon, and certainly before we start the trial on Monday. There was a recent request, motion, by the Prosecution for the joint hearing of evidence common to this case, Brdjanin and Talic, and also Stakic. And the decision relating to that motion has been taken. It was filed last Friday. The motion was rejected. I would imagine that the Prosecution is aware of that decision already. I wonder if the Defence have been served with a copy? You have. So, basically, you know that there is no question of hearing evidence -- evidence of witnesses common to both trials. But I understand, and we will come to this later on, it is my intention to visit the common terrain that exists between this trial and Stakic, which will come at a later stage. And this is a matter which I suppose we will need to discuss. In particular, I need to address the Prosecution in that regard, being sure that cooperation will be forthcoming because it is in the interest of the economy of justice and also in the interest of the efforts that have been made in that direction by the Office of the Prosecution. There is an appeal pending. Mr. Pitron, you know that the determination of that appeal does not depend on me. But I have obtained the necessary information, and I am confident that the appeal will be decided in time before the commencement of the trial on Monday. So that is something to await for, both on your part and as well on my part. There are -- there is a motion -- two motions by General Talic; one is to dismiss charges, and the other one for the dismissal of -- the declaration of the entire pretrial phase as null and void. The first of these two is basically ready. You will be served with the decision in real-time. The second one, in the Tribunal -- in the Chamber's opinion, deserves more attention, is being elaborated and will be finished before Monday. And the copy of the decision will be communicated to you before Monday. There is also an outstanding motion -- I'm anticipating you will bear patience with me. I am anticipating certain matters that I am sure you would have raised in any event. So I am pre-empting some of these issues beforehand so we can then go ahead as planned in the agenda that I have prepared for today's meeting. There is another outstanding motion filed by Mr. Brdjanin through his learned counsel. It was filed on the 13th of December. And that relates to an objection that has been raised with regard to Rule 92 bis procedure. I don't need to go into details. Again, that is a matter that has been studied thoroughly by myself together with the other two Judges, Schomburg and Mumba. Until now, they are the other two Judges forming part of this Trial Chamber. And a decision will be forthcoming by Monday, certainly not later than Monday. Also, Rule 92 bis is a matter which will be revisited later on in the course of this Pre-Trial Conference because we need to discuss a little bit further. There is an important piece of information that I wanted to give you. Way back in May of last year, Mr. Ackerman, Mr. de Roux, and Mr. Pitron, you were informed by the Prosecution that they had filed under seal a confidential motion pursuant to Rule 66(C). You know what Rule 66(C) is. I will not go into detail. I realised in the course of preparing for this trial conference, at least from the records that I had before me, that you had not been informed as to whether my predecessor, Judge Hunt, who was pre-trial Judge until last month, or until a month and a half ago, whether he had determined this issue or not. I am in a position now to give you the necessary information which you are entitled to certainly before the commencement of the trial because, however relevant or irrelevant it may be, it's important to know. After the filing of the motion on the 8th of May, 2001, Prosecution filed a supplementary motion just over a month later, on the 15th of June of last year. You were also, according to the information that I have, informed of the filing of this supplementary motion. There were some correspondence exchanged between the pre-trial Judge, my predecessor, and the Prosecution with regard to the content and substance of the original motion and the supplementary motion. And my predecessor gave his decision on a confidential and ex parte basis on the 3rd of October of last year. His decision is as follows: He found that there was nothing to demonstrate that the documents in question were likely to assist in the case of either of your -- either of the accused. As a consequence, he found that there was "no point in a minute examination in this decision" - that's the decision that he gave - "of each document to determine the validity of the Prosecution's claim that the disclosure to the accused would either harm the interest of the state of the country" - which is referred to in a confidential manner in the original motion, and I won't repeat the name of the country for obvious reasons - "or reveal the identity of vulnerable persons who would be put at risk." However, with regard to three documents -- and I don't think it is the case of referring to the identification of these documents simply because of what follows -- my predecessor directed the Prosecution to pursue the motion within 14 days of the filing of the last pre-trial briefs of the accused for consideration to be given to disclosure pursuant to Rule 68. It so happened that on 4th of December, 2001, the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber in a confidential ex parte memorandum that it did not intend to pursue its application and would, as a consequence, disclose the documents to the Defence. So basically, I have put my conscience at ease in this regard, and I have put you in a position at least you know how this matter was decided by my predecessor. It leads me to put a very simple and straightforward question, Ms. Korner, as to whether these three documents were eventually disclosed to the Defence as indicated by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were. I should add, Your Honour having read out a lot of this confidential ex parte motion in Court, that we, of course, keep under review as the Defence develops anything that may materialize. And if it clearly becomes relevant to any stage, then we will seek further guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I suppose there is nothing on the part of the Defence that you would like to add to close this particular chapter at this stage? I think the matter is concluded in any case. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. de Roux. Now, you were informed, barely a few days ago, like I was, that the Prosecution filed a motion to redact certain documents. This was filed, if I am correct -- anyway, the dates are not important. What I need to inform you at this particular stage is that this is being taken care of by myself with the assistance of my legal staff. I am going through the documentation and a decision will be forthcoming before the start of the trial. And of course, depending on that decision, you will receive or not receive documents that have been redacted or not redacted. I mean, that stands to be decided in due course, but I wanted you to know that it's being taken care of and will be decided in the next few days. By Friday, I think we will have a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention in relation to the particular motions which are connected, one of which Your Honour has granted in relation to protective measures, it is a matter the Prosecution would like to revisit for one matter and Mr. Cayley will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I was coming to that motion or that decision later on, and I realise that this is very much connected, and you realise also that in deciding this motion for the redacted documents, we had, of course, to take into consideration what we decided in regard to the other motion for the protective measures. And I understand also that there are other points that need to be raised and, of course, they will receive all my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm coming to that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While I'm on my feet, may I just ask, because Your Honour is running through the outstanding motions, did Your Honour get a copy of the five motions that were filed this morning by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I have heard about them but I haven't seen them yet, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, may I say this straight away to Your Honour, it may be advisable if Your Honour were to be given copies immediately, because they have a dramatic effect and would need -- they are something that need to be decided straight away, I'm afraid, on the start of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave this for the moment until I will suspend the hearing for some time, until I take proper cognizance of the substance. More or less I see what they are and why you very rightly say that they have to be decided in the very first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make it absolutely clear the reason I'm raising it now is the first witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reason I'm raising it now -- I don't know how long this conference is going to last, but the first witness who is mentioned is going to be on a plane, at very large cost, from the United States tomorrow if Mr. Ackerman -- if -- sorry, I'll start that one again, unless Your Honour accedes to this motion that Mr. Ackerman has put in. So it is something, as I say, I'm slightly surprised that Your Honour wasn't given a copy this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. This morning I had a very lengthy conference in preparation for this hearing, and it may be my fault because documents were coming in the tray, but I was not advised that there were new documents. If I had been, I would have read them or gone through them in the very little time that I had available. But I promise you, I will suspend the hearing for a while and will take proper cognizance of them, and if necessary to reconvene tomorrow morning, we will reconvene tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure, Your Honour, that the record would show that they were filed late yesterday afternoon, not this morning. I filed them as quickly as I could after getting the Prosecution's witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, which actually -- we are coming straight into that. A few days ago, or just two days ago, actually, I received a copy of a motion by the Prosecution with regard to the statement of the expert witness mentioned in that motion, to which I understand one of your five motions refers. I will just -- and I see also there is also a reply, a response on the part of General Talic. Have you received a copy of the response on the part of General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's not -- doesn't cause quite the same problems because the only request is they want to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what is your reaction to it, before I enter into Mr. Ackerman's motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I understand, and I've read it in French obviously, the attitude of General Talic's counsel is that they want him here because they intend to cross-examine. Well, that's fine. They are not suggesting a delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But cross-examination is one thing and taking his statement sort of as read is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The point that they make, as indeed did Mr. Ackerman rightly, is that we didn't disclose until Monday of this week two previous transcripts of evidence that he's given here before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to that, it is right to say, and I say that straight away, his latest report, the translation into the Bosnian language will be available on Friday morning. So, Your Honour, that's, as I say, the real problem. The expert is about to travel here from the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards this issue, we have just received this very moment these materials from the Prosecution. Obviously, I have not been able to familiarise myself with them as of yet. I just want to say that this is something which has become a habit here on the part of the Prosecution, to disclose at the last minute masses of documents, some of which the Prosecution has had for a long time. We have already objected to this way of operating. I have no response to give to all those documents so long as I haven't read them, and that will require some time, some time to read them, obviously. Your Honour, since I have the floor, if you allow me, I would like to go back to two points in the objections that we raised. You did say that you were going to rule on those preliminary motions by Monday. These are important preliminary motions, all the more so because the Prosecution blames or accuses General Talic for having given orders allegedly to subordinates or to -- orders that were not carried out by the subordinates, and we still do not have the identity of the perpetrators of the crimes and offences that have been put forward. This is very serious for the Defence because we are responsible vis-a-vis those who carried out orders. We don't know if there were people who were carrying out orders that were given, who committed or didn't commit the various crimes. And that I think that this point must be settled before the hearing because this is part of the indictment, this is part of the substantive way which my client stands accused, and we cannot properly prepare his defence so long as this essential point on which the Prosecution has always shown some reluctance to give information, despite the many questions that your predecessor Judge Hunt put forward. The Prosecution never wanted to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. respond to the questions and those essential questions. And that I think this discussion has to be settled as a preliminary issue in accordance with Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a reaction to that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours is going to rule on the two motions, and I await the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But in any case, this particular accusation that is being thrown at you, that you have persistently sort of refused to indicate the perpetrators or the agents, if you can call them agents, used by -- or that the various accusations refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been the subject, as Mr. de Roux rightly says, of a number of discussions. Judge Hunt ruled, and it has been echoed in a number of different cases, that where you're dealing with high-level, as it were, officials, remote from the actual scene of the crime, it is unnecessary to state in the indictment the identity of the people actually committing the crime. This indictment has been described as the "War and Peace" of indictments, and to do that would make it war and peace and anarchy put together. In the pre-trial brief, we have set out our case in 150 pages, very clearly explaining what it is. In each of the statements, all of which have been disclosed to the Defence in full, it sets out, where there is an allegation of killing, who actually did the killing. Now, of course, Your Honour, if I were ordered to do that, I could go through each and every one of the statements and I could write out what I hope most people would be able to read for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in any case, it's more or less, in my opinion, partly, at least, it has been visited already by my predecessor in some of his decisions. And more or less, I think it will be addressed also in the decision that I will be taking by the end of the week. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I should tell Your Honour that there is no other indictment, or was not until this indictment, which contains the amount of detail which is in this particular indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll for the moment suspend the debate on the motion on the expert witness until I go through a motion filed by Mr. Ackerman yesterday, and go to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before Your Honour leaves that, could I just mention one other matter: The motions themselves mentioned the names of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask, I appreciate that we said that we weren't going to be seeking protective measures for these witnesses in our list. The problem, however, is that occasionally witnesses arrive and matters have changed and ask for protective measures. So I would ask if there are future filings, that they be done with the number which has been allocated to the witness rather than the witness's name. And Your Honour, that number appears in the Rule 65 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that you will agree to that, Mr. de Roux? I didn't anticipate a no. So that will be sorted out. I now suggest or propose to you to go through various points that I have -- various matters and issues that I have prepared, some of which follow up from the previous Pre-Trial Conference, and some of which are new. And I will start with those which are a follow-up of what we discussed last time. One matter that was discussed here in this Chamber was with regard to any facts that, after due consultation, you may agree upon, facts in issue obviously that you may agree upon. Has there been a -- some sort of development in this area?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to tell you, Your Honour, that despite Your Honour's plea that we should cooperate, it has not been possible to do that, for a number of reasons. I wrote a letter requesting a meeting, which was declined, or various conditions were imposed on the -- if there was to be a meeting, which were in my view wholly unacceptable. It included dropping charges if there was to be a meeting. Your Honour, we served on the Defence a document which I will now hand in to Your Honour. Your Honour, I have a copy here. Your Honour, I could go through what the Defence are prepared to agree; it amounts to virtually nothing. I think about the only fact that General Talic is prepared to agree, or his counsel are prepared to agree, is in connection with his biography, and not even that is agreed in full. The same effectively -- although may I say Mr. Ackerman is prepared to agree a few more, not very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. de Roux, if this is the position, let's not waste time on it. You know, I made an appeal last time. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to waste any time. We've got to be serious here. When an agreement is asked for, one tries to retain a minimum of objectivity, and one does not ask in 15 pages for an accused to accuse himself. The points for which the Prosecution was asking for agreements, obviously, was tantamount to a self-accusation, and that cannot be part of an interpretation which is as subjective, not only in respect of the facts but the very history of the Balkans. I think we have got to be serious and reasonable. We cannot agree to proposals that were made to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will be very brief. I need to tell you, as I have told Ms. Korner over and over, there are numerous outstanding translations yet in this case. There are many, many documents that I can't read. There are many, many documents that my client can't read. And that is a major problem in trying to arrive at any kind of agreement with regard to anything that we might be willing to agree upon. It would be irresponsible of me to start entering into any agreements at this point until I know what this case is about. It is frightening that we are going to go to trial on Monday, and I don't know what's in these documents. And I should. To be a good lawyer, I should. But I can't because the translations have not been done. As we get into the witnesses, the problems are legion with regard to the witnesses because the translations have not been done. You will read in my motions that all the witnesses -- virtually all the witnesses, with the exception of two that are listed by the Prosecutor to be the initial witnesses, the translations have not been done. My client can't read their statements. I can't read some of their statements. How on earth can we proceed? That is a gross violation of Article 21.4 and the case law with regard to it. And yet, we seem to be moving toward a trial start on the 21st with, I think, only two witness that could possibly be called because they are the only two that we have been furnished the proper information with regard. And I kind of resent being accused by Ms. Korner of not being willing to cooperate with regard to agreements when it's the Prosecution who has not given us the material that would make it possible for us to do that in a responsible and reasonable way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we leave it at that? I think, at this point in time, I would rather not waste more time on this. More or less, it will be an exercise in one trying to justify oneself, and let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I only want to say this: You'll see a list of documents that Mr. Ackerman allegedly hasn't received. I think he's in error about a lot of them. But it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I mean, Ms. Korner. Because if we start exchanging arguments and opinions on this matter, I can foresee it's not going to come to an end quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't matter. In fact, we have got signed receipts from Mr. Ackerman for most of these documents. But the point is, as I think I made earlier, it isn't so much those witnesses that matter at this stage. It is the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to that, there is a very simple solution; he will give evidence viva voce here in court. Forget about the transcript. But then, of course, if I had in mind a time frame for the next, say, three weeks, four weeks or whatever, I mean, that will have to change obviously, because I want to push forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the point is, it is intended that he should give evidence, but what -- the objection is that there is insufficient time for them to consider the material, although I confess that I find it quite surprising, because in essence, the expert has testified on a number of occasions saying effectively more or less the same thing. There are -- there are additions in this report which are specific to this case, but the background he has testified about, I think, on three separate occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's deal with another matter. Sorry, Mr. de Roux? Please go ahead. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] But you see, this is an example. I don't wish to enter into a polemics, but saying that this is a historical expert used by the Prosecution who always gives his version of history, that's interesting, one could say. This witness has already testified in three other trials. Why have we not been served with his transcripts? We received the day before yesterday 300 pages beginning with the year 600. This is very interesting, but on these old facts of history, there are so many counter-experts, specialists on the Balkans, who could testify. This is very interesting, but it would be much simpler if we had received a copy of the transcript of the statement of this professor in this Tribunal, as he has already testified three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will decide on that in any case. Matters of disclosure. You will recall that at the last Pre-Trial Conference, and throughout all the Status Conferences that have taken place until then, the question of disclosure had come up. I would first refer to disclosures under Rule 66(A)(ii) and I would ask for an update. Ms. Korner, for example, just to give you a hand, during the last Pre-Trial Conference, you had mentioned that it was your intention to call two additional witnesses, namely an investigator and a witness with respect to crime-based evidence. I will mention them one by one so you can answer or give me information with regard to this one at least first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The crime-based? In fact, Your Honour, there will be no further statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then you had also informed the Tribunal that due to translation delays, there were two statements that had not yet been disclosed. Actually, it was translation from English into Bosnian language that was still being awaited for. Any news about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour, I'm just trying to find out. Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, it's slightly more difficult because we've been conducting witness searches, and other statements have come up, but as I understand the position, all statements taken by the Tribunal investigators have now been disclosed with translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is that I say this sometimes and then it turns out that something slipped through the net, but -- so I will do a double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Next, you will recall the diary. We had information forthcoming from the OTP and an explanation as to the problems encountered at the time. I was informed on that occasion by you that it was anticipated that by Monday, 21st January, only about 300 pages would have been translated. Is that still the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And will they be translated? Will they be ready, those 300 pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have already I think disclosed as -- we have been getting them back in dribs and drabs and we have been disclosing them as we get them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then in the course of the last Pre-Trial Conference, you had also informed the Chamber that your office was still conducting searches with respect to about over 100 witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- who you had the intention to call, in order to determine if these are mentioned in other statements or had made statements to other authorities. At the time, that's in December, you said 32 searches had been completed but not yet reviewed and 42 searches were still to be completed. Can you give us an update on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the searches are still going on. We have had unfortunately the Christmas period intervening. We've disclosed material in relation to each of the witnesses that we intend to call relating to Banja Luka, but we are still completing the searches. In other words, we are doing a double-check to make sure things don't slip through the net.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Before I close this particular part on Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosures, any of the Defence counsel would like to make any comments in this regard as to what Ms. Korner has just stated? Yes, Mr. Pitron?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very briefly, Your Honour. We have received a certain number of exhibits from the Prosecutor which we are still receiving and apparently some of them have been in her possession since July, 1997, but never mind. I understand that some documents that will be disclosed are being translated and that they are not ready yet. I understand, but I may be wrong, that there will be other documents which we need to receive from the Prosecutor relative to testimony from Banja Luka, the first testimony that we are due to hear. So some have been received, some are being translated, we haven't received them, and there are additional documents which we will need to have, are still not in our possession and have not been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is as much a problem -- that is as much a problem to you, as I understand. I am fully aware how much of a problem it is, but it's also a problem to the Prosecution, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm not prosecuting anyone. I am defending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I spent a considerable time of my career where you are, so I know your problems. I'm coming to Rule 68 disclosures now. Ms. Korner, again, I'm sorry to ask you -- to make you have to stand up and sit down. You will recall that during the last Pre-Trial Conference, you had informed me that, more or less, you had completed the Rule 68 disclosures of all documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think we said we had completed all the obvious Rule 68 from the collections. We were making a search, however, of other material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You had told me at the time that you were still dealing with notes, as distinguished from signed statements, kept by investigators of conversations with people plus reports of investigations into Mount Vlasic and Bosanski Petrovac. That's the information that results from your statement last time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't reread in detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry, but what I actually want to know is whether, with regard to what was pending then, there are still documents which are -- have not yet been disclosed, or whether everything, to your knowledge, has now been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Documents that we have found containing Rule 68, that we have found, and I emphasise that, and Rule 68 as best as we have been able to guess it, because we don't know what the defence is, is -- has been completed, but that the searches of notes and the like is still continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You just mentioned because you don't know what the defence is. Incidentally, you will recall, Mr. Ackerman, that -- you may sit down for the moment. I will give you the opportunity. I just want to deal with something important but which relates to Mr. Ackerman more than anything -- anyone else. You had filed your pre-trial brief on behalf of your client, and there had been an objection raised by the Prosecution. That is being decided. In fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've ruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you been served with a copy? Okay. And in this regard, and before I give the floor to Mr. de Roux, is there anything -- or rather, leave that. Leave that. And I think I can give the floor -- I'm having an afterthought on something, but I can visit that later on. For the moment, I can ask Mr. de Roux to say what he was planning to say. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Very brief, regarding Rule 68, we have received a certain number of documents on the 15th of January, documents under Rule 68, on the 15th of January. And we learned at the same time that the Prosecution investigators were questioning, in Banja Luka, a certain number of individuals who could be witnesses, and we would like to have the integral recordings of the investigations or interviews conducted quite recently, which we are not aware of, as those interviews occurred some 15 days ago, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are doing exactly what we were ordered to do last time by Judge Hunt, which is go through those interviews and disclose anything in them which may be of Rule 68. That Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. will happen. It's simply a question the investigators are at the moment re-listening to the tapes. Anything that is Rule 68 will be disclosed, as we did with the last witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to, again, Rule 68 disclosure, is there anything else that you would like to raise at this point, before I move to something else? Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I'm confused. There were some interviews done by the Prosecutor of several persons in Banja Luka, many of them who were members of the Crisis Staff, and my recollection is that when we discussed that in the presence of Judge Hunt, the Prosecutor said that they were getting the transcripts done and would give us the transcripts of those interviews as soon as they were completed. And I'm quite sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not my recollection, at least from what I heard during the exchange of views on this matter during the Pre-Trial Conference in December in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll read the transcript and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because my -- and I have quite the vivid recollection of what was stated, was that some tapes had been heard and transcripts made ready, and they would be made available. Other tapes were still not heard again, and they needed to be heard. And then there was an assurance coming on the part of the Prosecution that whatever falls under Rule 68 would be disclosed. However, I remember also that Ms. Korner did not let the opportunity pass by without taking advantage of it and remind you of your constant complaints that you were being inundated with material under Rule 68 pretext irrespective of whether it was exculpatory or not. Anyway, I mean, in order to lessen the burden, they would -- so in other words, that's my vivid recollection. I stand to be corrected. As usual, I am far from infallible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you revisited it more recently than the rest of us probably, so I'm sure you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I take it as a commitment on your part, Ms. Korner, that anything that needs to be disclosed under Rule 68 will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to make it absolutely clear, we are not going to disclose the full transcripts; we are going to disclose the Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You made that clear last time, and I think it was taken as that, how it should be. I will move to reciprocal disclosure, and you will recall that this was more or less a little bit hotly debated last time. And more or less what we agreed upon is this: I suggested during the last Pre-Trial Conference to you, Mr. Ackerman, in particular, because this arose as a result of your pre-trial brief, and there was in my opinion an agreement to the effect that there will be reciprocal disclosure on a rolling basis. What I want to know is if you have anything to tell me about the current status of this rolling reciprocal disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I this morning -- sorry, this afternoon, received a bundle of documents from Mr. Ackerman, which I understand is part of reciprocal disclosure. Despite letters reminding counsel for General Talic of Your Honours' ruling, we've received nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Either Mr. Pitron or Mr. de Roux.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have sent 51 documents to the Prosecutor, which obviously didn't arrive. They were sent yesterday or the day before, and they will probably arrive within the same time limit as the 500 pages that we received today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of these --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely totally, wholly unaware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have no reason to doubt that they have been sent, so it's a question of... You will have the same problem that the Defence has. You will have to do a lot of reading between now and Monday, and so will I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Expert witnesses. This, I am going to come to later on. Okay. Forensic evidence. Again, this is a follow-up. You will recall -- I will be very brief on this -- for reasons that appear to me and to the majority of you to be very obvious at the time during the past -- the previous Pre-Trial Conference, I had suggested that an agreement on the formal proof of that was possible and that it would on a prima facie basis at least wasn't likely to deprive the Defence from anything, and there would still be the right of the Defence to ask for the production of evidence with regard to any particular death of any particular person. And on the part of Mr. Brdjanin, there was consensus. And in regard to General Talic, Mr. Pitron had requested some time to think about it. Are you in a position, or have you been busy reading the piles of documents sent to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been answered. That's the one thing that we got an answer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They say they do not dispute the information but reserve the right to do subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. So I thank the Defence Bench for -- Defence team for General Talic for the cooperation shown. And witness from humanitarian organisations, you know that a decision has been handed, which I suppose you have a copy of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we -- we want to revisit that issue, and we would like to go into closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into closed session now. More or less, I have an indication of what is to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cayley is going to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner, private or closed? What do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it should be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Closed session, I would rather tend to agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Private session essentially -- if we go into closed session, then we have to pull the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be safer to go to -- because I expect to -- I expect to hear things that I would rather -- I feel more at ease if we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one more minute before you start. I need to dig up the decision. Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for this document, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention, we have added to, Your Honour, but I haven't -- because there doesn't appear to be much opportunity to speak to the Defence, there is one witness that was missed off the list that they've got, which is Witness 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 74, yes. Incidentally, with regard to this list, Mr. Ackerman, please follow me in this, I notice that 7.221, 7.64 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can tell you, Your Honour, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, simply because we had the unfortunate filing of these five motions before the filing of your list, may I suggest that we find a quick way of going about it before Mr. Ackerman's motions get further distributed, because obviously your motions refer directly to the names of the persons. And with regard to those persons, now the Prosecution is seeking protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In fact, this hasn't had general distribution. The Registry very wisely got in touch with us when they received the motions, and although Mr. Ackerman hadn't asked for them to be filed confidentially, they have been filed confidentially. They are not available to the press office. At this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not that big of a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But only because, as I say, the Registry wisely asked us about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What further precautions need to be taken at this stage? Because the motion for protective measures has not yet been decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Ackerman looked at the list, clearly saw that we weren't at this stage applying for protective measures, and that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, so we are saved there. Okay, matter is closed. So we have no problem there. But I will keep this list readily available. I think we will have a break now of 15 minutes. What's the usual break? 15 to 20 minutes, and we will reconvene after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before Your Honour continues with the agenda, may I say that I'm happy to report that when I went upstairs in the adjournment, I found placed on my chair a parcel which contained the documents that General Talic's counsel has supplied us with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fifty-one of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't counted them, but Mr. Cayley is having a look. Your Honour, I think there was one other matter which I wanted to raise in connection with that but I don't seem to have made a note. But in any event, we do have the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just before I move to what I had on my agenda, I'd like to make a very quick reference to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, before we move to the other item on my agenda, Ms. Korner, please, I refer you to one of the motions by Mr. Ackerman referred to before; namely, that relating to the testimony of the expert you intend to present on the first day of the trial. I have read all five motions, but this is the motion that I would like to address your attention to for the time being. Having read this and having read your motion for the admission of the statement under Rule 94, which arrived in my chambers I think yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot when it was filed, but I think it was last week sometime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is an apparent discrepancy between what is contained in your motion and what is contained in Mr. Ackerman's motion in a sense that, according to what you state, Mr. Ackerman should have received the statement way back in December, and you specify the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman is saying something completely different. I suppose you have gone through his motion as I have. Later on, I will be revisiting this matter, so perhaps if you could have someone from your team that could dig up the documentation, the records that you have in your office, to establish precisely when -- because you were very categoric in your motion specifying different dates for different defendants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Ackerman is disputing that he got -- that he did get the statements. He's not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not disputing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I got a copy of the statement from them sometime long ago, and I thought I made that clear in my motion. Maybe I didn't. If I didn't, I intended to. I was referring to the actual filing with the Court, which is what the Rule -- the Rule speaks of filing with the Court, and the amount of time one has after that filing to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how does it affect you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't affect me at all, Your Honour. What affects me is there is no B/C/S translation and so my client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's been promised for Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How on earth can my client look at that and give me instructions? I can't even go see him over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's no justification for Mr. Donia not to come over and, if necessary, start giving evidence orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is. We have got hundreds and hundreds of pages of transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget about the hundreds of pages. He will come here and give evidence, and your client will have the evidence translated there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand if you want to make that ruling, you may do so, but it conflicts with four years of jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you think, but I am faced with the motion now, at the 11th hour, trying to stop Mr. Donia from coming over and start giving evidence in a trial where he is scheduled to be the first witness, and I'm just telling you there is a very simple solution. First of all, Rule 94, as amended now, gives me all the power to shorten time limits and provide for a solution in any case. But I think if that is the attitude that is going to be adopted, as long as you have had this document for more than 21 days, I don't see why you should raise the objection that you are raising simply because the Prosecution failed to provide the document to the Tribunal. That's the Tribunal's problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can make myself clear. I have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That is going to be solved by Friday and I can quite understand that that could still create a problem for you because on Friday you're going to say, "but I haven't had time to discuss it with" your client because it's in English, what you have, and what you will have on Friday will be in the language that your client understands, and it will give you the opportunity. Okay. We can obviate that. We can start with Mr. Donia coming over and giving oral evidence, and when you are in a position to admit the statement as presented, as filed by Ms. Korner, we will go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make myself clear, Your Honour, so that there is no misunderstanding. It's my belief that it is the law of this Tribunal that witness statements and material that's provided in addition to those witness statements that involve other statements of the witness are required by the law of this Tribunal to be in the language of the accused. None of the transcripts that have been provided with regard to Mr. Donia are in the language of the accused. One of the statements provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Ackerman. I don't think you are reading me in the loud and clear manner that I think -- I thought for a moment I had been. I am telling you I have in front of me a motion from Ms. Korner, which admittedly is based, as it is, also as a result of the fact that the Tribunal had not been furnished with a copy of the statement, as it should have been. There is also the specific request contained in that motion. In response to that motion, I have two documents, one from the Defence team for General Talic saying, "Mr. Donia has given evidence in two, three other trials. We should have had this available. We insist on a cross-examination." Well, I'm not saying how I will decide on that issue, but it will be decided. You come along with another argument, saying, "The Tribunal has not been given a copy of the statement of Mr. Donia when it should have been given, and it has been given a copy at this very late hour. The Tribunal's problem has become my problem but it has become my problem because the copy which I have had for the past three weeks is in English and not in Bosnian." How the two can be reconciled together or can be put in the same basket together to provide you with an excuse for asking the delay of the production of Mr. Donia as a witness, I don't understand. However, if that is indeed a problem to you, and if indeed your client finds objection to Mr. -- to the admission of the document because it is in English and when it will be in Bosnian, it will be, according to you, too late for you to consult, scrap it. There will be no statement, written statement, from Mr. Donia. He will be brought forward, presented as a witness, and we will hear his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In English or whichever language he speaks, and it will be translated in B/C/S, as your client is entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not - and I repeat - I am not talking about whether a document can be admitted or not. What I'm talking about is the Prosecution's obligation to provide material to the Defence in a timely manner, both in English or French and in the language of the accused. That has not been done with regard to this witness. Now, just yesterday - just yesterday, Your Honour - I receive additional statements of this witness, and I don't know how many pages, 700, 800, maybe, pages of transcript from testimony he's given in other proceedings. This case is two and a half years old. I suspect several months ago that they knew they were going to call Robert Donia as a witness and yet they waited until yesterday to give me material that I need to prepare for cross-examination. Now, that's not fair, that's not proper, and it's not translated into B/C/S as the Rules and the law of this Tribunal require so that my client can look at it and knows what's coming. 21(4) requires that he is to be advised of the nature of the charges against him, and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is that includes the statements of witnesses who the Prosecution will call, and those statements must be in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent right, but on Friday, this will be available in the language that your client understands. And if needs be, there will be a delay in calling upon you for cross-examination, but not in the production of the witness because the witness will be testifying viva voce in any case. Listen, Mr. Ackerman, I am in the same position as you are. The document was presented to me, not on the 26th of December but only yesterday, will have to be read by me together with piles of other documents between now and Monday. But I will sit down or lie down and read them. I have to, because otherwise I will come here completely unprepared, and I have never done that in my life, or in my career. God knows how many hundreds, if not thousands, of pages I have read already. And sometimes pages which I know probably may not be that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it's the position of Your Honour that with witnesses as to whom the Prosecution has failed to comply in terms of the provision of material and properly translated material, that cross-examination can be reserved until that material is available, then I have no further argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, because I think we ought to get to know each other a little bit better, the way I conduct trials is pretty straightforward. If there is work to be done, it will be done. Now, I realise that things could and should have been better conducted. I mean, I see no reason why, for example, such a mistake should have taken place. But it has taken place. If you ask me whether between delaying the beginning of the trial because it has happened, it has taken place, or whether I will make a sacrifice and read that document notwithstanding that it has only arrived on my desk barely 24 hours ago, I will sit down and read it and make sure that the trial will start. But these are the two options. You were not deprived -- your client, in other words, will certainly not be deprived of the opportunity of conducting a cross-examination in a timely manner. But to ask me to delay the production or the bringing over of Mr. Donia simply because this has not yet arrived on your desk in B/C/S and you haven't had an opportunity to discuss it with your client, that doesn't make sense. What makes sense is let's bring him here just the same. He will start giving evidence. Your client will have time to read the document in his language, if he wants to read it in his language, and you will have ample time to discuss it or debate it with him. In the meantime, there will be the evidence coming in from Mr. Donia, and we will take it from there. But delaying the bringing over of the witness for the reasons that you bring forward in your motion, and especially because I have been only given a copy of the transcript of the statement now and not when you got it, it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as long as you're prepared to have him come back in a month or two so I can do my cross, then I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you're saying in a month or two. I will be the one to decide whether it's time or whether you should be in a position to conduct the cross-examination, not you. You may stand up at any given moment and say, "I am not in a position to conduct the cross-examination," but it will be I and my two other colleagues who will decide whether you should be in a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. I'm telling you. You may tell me, "I haven't had time to read this," but rest assured that I will find the time to read it by Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I read that a long time ago. But I have nine documents that they gave me that are in Serbo-Croat that I can't read. How can I cross-examine when I can't read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have a translator, or interpreter. I don't. I don't think he has finished, Mr. Pitron. Let him finish first, and then you can take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I kind of have finished. I think the position that we are in is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I realise that you are in a difficult position. I mean, I will be the first one, and please accept it in the most definitive of terms. I realise that you three are in a very difficult position, but so am I. This is why last time I told you, let's start with a clean slate. There are difficulties. This is not an easy trial, but this is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also a trial that is not going to begin one day and finish the next. This is a trial which is going to be divided into phases according to municipalities. What applies to one municipality need not necessarily apply to another. And we can start with one municipality, and certain other things may stay in abeyance and be done, in the meantime pending which you will have time then to prepare for the next municipality and the next municipality as we go along. However, please don't try to take over and dictate the way -- or the time when the cross-examination should be conducted, or whether you are prepared -- you are entitled to say, "I am not prepared now," and it's up to the Tribunal to decide whether you should or ought to have been prepared by then. If you can rest assured also that if I believe that your objection or that your claim to not have enough time is justified, I will grant you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I attached to one of my motions a piece of transcript from the Omarska case, and I know you haven't had a chance to go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it dealt with a situation where the Prosecutor realised that they had failed to provide some of the materials in association with a witness in the language of the accused and therefore said to the Court, we can't go forward with this witness until we've done that. Ms. Hollis, who has been -- who had been there at the time for more than five years, very familiar with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, was very embarrassed, apologized to the Tribunal for not having provided all of the materials with regard to that witness in the language of the accused. She believed that it had been done. The Court said, We have no alternative but to adjourn this case until those are provided and Defence counsel have an opportunity to study them. As Judge Rodrigues said at the conclusion of his remarks in that, "We cannot, in the interest of efficiency, fail in terms of fairness." And let's not do that. I don't mind going forward with this case, but I will insist that my client's rights be protected in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They will be protected, Mr. Ackerman, but not at the expense of mixing two issues together when they belong separately. One of the arguments that you bring forward is, Your Honour, it's not fair that you have received this document now. And please look at Rule 94 as amended. Mr. Donia cannot be produced to give evidence on Monday. I'm sorry, where is the nexus? Where does it follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Rule was amended to read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How does it follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe the Rule was amended after the prior Rule's 21-day deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Rules as amended give me -- give the Tribunal, rather than me, much more leeway and flexibility, together also with Rule 127, than this Tribunal ever had under the previous Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's my position that the Rule enlarges the time rather than narrowing it, but that's up to a Chamber to decide, not me. I can make the argument at least. But I think I've completed the things I needed to say with regard to that, Your Honour, and I understand that I'll be given time to prepare for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. You don't even have to doubt that. And I will conduct the orchestra as needs be, pacing it as necessary, to make sure that your client's rights are guaranteed. There will not be any undue pressure. There will be pressure, but not undue pressure. Mr. Pitron?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when listening to you speak with Mr. Ackerman, I was wondering whether you were speaking about the same documents. It is clear that we received reports and summaries of Mr. Donia's statements that are anticipated for next Monday. We received not long ago but we worked on what we did, we translated, and we're in a position to work with those documents. But what we're speaking about today is another document, the 800 pages, a little bit more if I've calculated right, which are also Mr. Donia's statements. And they deal with all of his testimony in this Tribunal in other cases and which are an integral part of the elements which will be used as of Monday by Mr. Donia and by the Prosecutor and by ourselves during cross-examination in order to try to bring light on the matter for the Tribunal. What we're saying, and now I agree with Mr. Ackerman, is that these documents will not be translated into Serbo-Croat by Monday. Let's be very clear about that. I mean that part, an important part - actually, an essential part of what Mr. Donia is going to say, because it's much more important than the summary that we have today, a very important part of what Mr. Donia is going to say will not be known to our client before he reads them. I believe that familiarity by myself and by my client of all of a witness's position before he testifies is absolutely essential for the general defence, both for me and for my client. It isn't by discovering what Mr. Donia is going to say when he does speak; that's not how we will be able to act effectively. And I think that by supporting this position, I am in complete harmony with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That is my point. And I want us to understand that we're speaking about the 800 pages that we received today and not about the 50 or 100 that we received on the 26th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean, I think we are mixing issues here. Those 800-odd pages that you are referring to, as I understand, do not constitute or form an integral part of the statement that the Prosecution in its motion is asking to be produced. Obviously, these are documents that you may require or you may -- you feel you may need for the purposes of cross-examination. You will be given all the ample opportunity and time necessary or required for you to take cognizance of those documents and be able to make your cross-examination at the right time, but don't ask me to pre-empt every issue now, beforehand, before we have even started, and say, "Those are 800 new documents which I don't even have myself." I mean, you have 800 pages; I don't even have them. But the thing is, as soon as I have those 800 pages, I will also be in a better position - you will immediately understand what I am telling you now - I will be in a better position to appreciate and give weight to what you are saying now. And if they are indeed necessary -- if they are a repetition of what there is in the statement that the Prosecution has filed with its motion, that's one thing. If there are other matters, that's another. But from what Ms. Korner said earlier on, I understand that the statement that has -- is purported to be made by Mr. Donia in this particular case is over and above what he stated in other cases, because it covers territory or events related to this particular case, which had nothing to do with previous cases. Well, I have to see those 800 pages, but obviously, you can take it from me, as from now, that if you require -- if they are required for cross-examination purposes, you will, of course -- I have to take into consideration that you need to read 800 pages, and you will have time to read 800 pages, but I will decide how much time, not you. This is the point I want to make. So what I resent is telling, you have to be prepared to summon Mr. Donia again in a month's time, if necessary even in three months' time, if necessary even more than once, if necessary even more than once, but I will be the one to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's be clear, please. It was never my intention to try to ask you to set any particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't. Mr. Ackerman did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I do agree with the fears that Mr. Ackerman expressed. What I was saying is my client must have the best Defence possible. You understand my concern that five days from the start of the trial, when I see that, as you just said that I'm going to discover in the 800 pages new facts that would change your vision and my vision of the trial, whereas these documents, some of them in any case, are dated June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, you are 100 per cent right, but you also realise that the point you are making now is completely different to the point that Mr. Ackerman made. Mr. Ackerman asks the Tribunal to delay the production of Mr. Donia as a witness. And that's a completely different matter. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I explain -- first of all deal with Mr. Ackerman's point? If Mr. Ackerman's expression is that the Prosecution waited until yesterday to hand over the previous record of the Court hearings of Mr. Donia, then he knows that is wrong if the suggestion is that was deliberate. He and I had a conversation in which I told him that I was sure he had been sent all previous transcripts. He informed me that was incorrect, and I, having checked, saw that he in fact was correct and I was wrong. It is unfortunate, it was just before Christmas or in the -- just after Christmas when we made the disclosure. We disclosed the previous transcript in which he testified in the case that is presently going on in this building involving the accused from Bosanski Samac. We omitted, through an error, which is our fault, my fault, to provide also the transcript of his testimony in the case of the Prosecutor against General Blaskic and his testimony in the case of the Prosecutor against Kordic and Cerkez. That was rectified this Monday. The transcripts were placed in the Defence locker. They are long; that is undoubtedly right. In essence, Dr. Donia's report, each of the reports that he has compiled, has, if I can put it that way, a relatively standard beginning which describes the history going back to 600 AD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've started reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was entirely my fault. Unfortunately, I did not read Rule 94 carefully enough, and although we sent it to the Defence before Christmas, we omitted to file it with the Court. Therefore, it is right to say that the Defence have only had the two other transcripts, Blaskic and Kordic, since Monday, but they have had the testimony in Bosanski Samac since before Christmas. Your Honour, I'm told that we have obtained the tapes from the Registry in respect of those two hearings in the Bosnian Serb language. That is being listened to at the moment by an interpreter to check where the evidence begins on the tape and where it ends. Copies will then be made and those -- therefore the translation or the audio recording of what is said in the Bosnian Serb language will be available to counsel on Friday. The extra documents that Dr. Donia refers to in his report, which we supplied with his report, again, we are fairly confident that the translation of those extra documents into English, because they are in Bosnian language, will be available on Friday. Now, may I say that my only concern is this, having heard what Your Honour has said: Dr. Donia, as Your Honour can see, is a professional man and has other engagements. As I understand Your Honour's proposal, it is that he should testify in chief and then cross-examination will be reserved until such time as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's if the current objections to the admission of this statement that you filed stand or are accepted by the Tribunal, because there is the other option which I suggested also, and that is admitting the document, the statement, providing the Defence time to go through it, and during that time, Mr. Donia would start giving evidence on whatever he can give evidence viva voce. In other words, there is absolutely nothing to -- how long were you envisaging his stay would take?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, one of the many questions I was going to ask under the heading "Witnesses" on your agenda was if any estimate could be given for the length of time these witnesses were going to be here, because we need to make arrangements. Effectively - and this is a matter that I would have liked to discuss at some stage with Defence counsel - I need to know what parts of the report are disputed and what are not, and I was proposing to take him through, briefly, in chief, only those parts that were disputed or that seemed to be particularly relevant. In other words, I had no intention of delving in open court with the witness into the history of Bosnia going back to 600. It's in the report; it can be read. So at the moment, I'm at somewhat of a loss to know what is to happen. As I say, it's exceedingly expensive to fly him over from the States. It will be even more expensive if he has to fly back again and then come back again for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is not a situation that has been brought about by the Tribunal or by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Your Honour, that, at the moment -- in any event, as I say, I don't know what's disputed, what's not, and how much I need to go into it. I would have anticipated that -- I'm sorry, I'm afraid I think it's customary while one counsel is on their feet for another one to remain sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will not be allowed to interrupt you, Ms. Korner. Please go ahead. He is French anyway. He knows what courtesy is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I was about to say, therefore, Your Honour, it has been exceedingly difficult, and I raise this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I realise that, Ms. Korner. I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I say the difficulty I want to refer to -- Your Honour has suggested that we try and agree matters. It is very difficult to discuss and agree matters if counsel decline to have a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would have been my first preference, but obviously we failed there. What I suggest we do is this, because I think that in any case, we cannot waste time. Given the current situation, I think that postponing the arrival of Mr. Donia doesn't make sense. On the other hand, approaching the matter in the way that you had intended in the first place, given the current -- the present situation, I also think doesn't make sense, in the sense that you, before or until now, you had expected to bring over Mr. Donia, you had expected to have on your table or on your desk a situation whereby everyone is prepared, and if there are questions that need to be addressed to him, they will be addressed either by the Prosecution or in cross-examination by the Defence. That obviously cannot happen first thing Monday morning. So what can happen Monday morning - and this will help you also make a choice now - what can happen Monday morning is that he will come over and he will start giving testimony, evidence, viva voce; if necessary, you will refer him to the statement that he has made bit by bit, and -- well, I mean, you will be gaining something very important, that whatever he will be saying at that point in time will be simultaneously translated in B/C/S, in B/C/S, and there will be less excuse on the part of the Defence that we still need to read what is contained in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it is necessary, he will read out the statement and automatically it's being translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say something? I don't know whether Your Honour intended to cut me off from making an opening, but I anticipate that I will be opening this case most of Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it is more probable -- I mean, it may well be that I don't take the whole morning, but I very much doubt that Dr. Donia would do anything more than really maybe possibly just start, but probably Tuesday morning, by which time, of course, the statement will have been translated and the Defence should have the tapes for their -- for the accused, of the previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But please do understand, we have all lived trials in our career, okay? I as a Judge, and as a previous lawyer, Defence counsel in this case, I can't expect either you or the Defence to do two things at a time. Yesterday, to give you an example, I had a phone call from my daughter, whose husband is a lawyer, as she is, and he is in charge of legal aid. He was called upon, given 24 hours' notice to defend an accused in a trial by jury because a lawyer who had been engaged before simply renounced the brief, one hour or two hours before the trial was supposed to start. The Judge wouldn't -- he said, "Okay, you can't afford another lawyer; I will appoint Dr. So and So to defend you." He appointed my son-in-law, who was furious.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's happened to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Gradually, he obtained a two-day grace. But he had to accept, and they did something for formality's sake on the first day, and now it's adjourned. And in the meantime, he can read and do a little bit of homework. But expecting him to do two things, or me expecting Mr. de Roux or Mr. Pitron or Mr. Ackerman to do two things, prepare for the trial, concentrate on what goes on Monday morning while you are -- and at the same time, listen to the tapes or consult with the client, it's -- that's not what I want to do.
