And this is why I was angry at you, Mr. Ackerman, because I don't think -- last time, we were on the same level or same wavelength. Today we weren't. Today you were asking for the pound of flesh, which you will never get from me. I am making myself clear to you and to the Prosecution. I mean, let's be reasonable. Let's start, but also be considerate, patient, and reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, I'm going to make the following suggestion: If everything is delivered to the Defence in either English, the documents they are waiting for, and in the Bosnian language Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for the tapes of the previous transcript, if the case were to be put back for the Wednesday, I'm asking, would that be sufficient time for them to deal with it? Because, Your Honour, it seems to me more sensible, if I may so, if that is the situation, for Dr. Donia to come, start his evidence, and to be cross-examined upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you live with that? Now, don't tell me that's not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're told that there are some tapes that will appear in our boxes sometime on Friday that have the testimony of Mr. Donia in prior cases in B/C/S and that that will satisfy the requirements of the Statute of this Tribunal and the law thereunder because our clients can simply sit and listen to those tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Satisfy the letter of the law, let's put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, those tapes, I don't know how many hours it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it may be more than the entire weekend, and that's how much time they apparently have to listen to these, and then have an opportunity to discuss with us what they have heard on the tapes. I just think it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But also, Mr. Ackerman, let's talk the same language now. You have seen the witness's statement. I'm not referring to those 800 pages. I'm referring to what I got and what you got as well. Out of those 150 pages -- something like that, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, what was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The length of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It amounts to -- the actual report itself is something like 77 pages, and then there's some annexes, maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Annexes, et cetera, yes. Let's talk the same language. And I am sure you're going to understand me. A substantial part of that report refers to events which are interesting to know and which go back centuries, which I don't think your client or yourself is going to be very much interested in cross-examining Mr. Donia about. You know which events I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When some of our ancestors were probably living on the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are other -- then there are other events on which I would expect a serious Defence team to cross-examine Mr. Donia thoroughly. I think you need more than Monday to go through those parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I seriously doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not referring to the 800 pages, because that's another matter. If you open the discussion there, I have already made the reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem, Judge, and I think we must be having problem communicating. Let me, first of all, apologise to you for suggesting that it might take 30 or 60 days. I wasn't trying to dictate a time to the Court when the Judge [sic] would come back. I was just estimating that I thought it might take us that long to be prepared, depending on how long it takes to get some of these other matters. But I doubt in the 800 pages of prior testimony any of it had to do with that ancient history that's contained in the report, and that's not what I'm concerned about. It would not surprise me to discover. And it would certainly be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are also going to discover that there is a lot of repetition in the three or four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect that's true. It would be folly for me to say, "I'm not going to read that material" because as soon as I don't, I'll learn after this case is over that he said something exactly the opposite in another case than what he is saying in this case. You know that can be, and I know that can be. And in fact, the chances of it are pretty high. I have to look at all that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't pass judgement on that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe you'll get to hear it, once I get to look at him when he's standing on the witness stand and I get to talk to him. But in any event, what I wanted to say is I think we are missing each other here. The issue that I am trying to bring to the Court's attention at this point is not an issue of whether that particular statement that has been filed in this case should be admitted or not. I don't care about that. You can admit it. You can do anything you want with it today. What I care about is this: It's the law of the Tribunal that the statements of witnesses and prior statements of witnesses and the attached material of witnesses must be provided both in a language of the Tribunal and in the language of the accused. Now, that means this 800 pages must be provided in the language of the accused. If you will look -- of course, you don't have the material yet. But if you will look, there's a witness by the name of Osman Sarak, who has prior testimony, and they have been provided it in B/C/S also because they know it must be provided in a language of the accused. Now, they are suggesting that the tapes will solve that. And I think that this Chamber and this Tribunal will probably agree with that, that the tapes will solve that requirement. The next problem, then, is my client is sitting out at the detention unit. He doesn't have a machine to play those tapes, so somebody will have to make the arrangements for him to be provided with a machine to play the tapes and provided with the ability and the facility to listen to them. And I think that that will probably solve that requirement, but it is a requirement that that material be provided in the language of the accused. And that's where I think you and I are missing each other. And that's true with all the witnesses. And when you look at the other motions that I filed, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't tell me that this is the first time that the question of having the defendant provided with a tape recorder has arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. To my knowledge, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would be very surprised if it's the first time it has arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the first time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my case, it's understandable. It was not bothering me in the least because if it's necessary, they will be made available. If necessary, I'll make an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You probably don't have to. I've never had to talk with the detention unit about providing tape recorders to defendants to listen to tapes. Maybe they do that routinely. And if they do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so. I mean, I would be very surprised if it's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If they do, that's fine. I just never heard of it. But in any event, I don't know how many hours of tapes there are. And Ms. Korner might not even know how many hours of tapes there are. But it's significant. If you just look at the 800 pages here, there are several full days of testimony there. And so you can't listen to that in a few hours. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you haven't answered my query, and my query was whether you have a response to the suggestion of Ms. Korner that instead of starting Monday, we start Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Starting the trial or just the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Starting the trial Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That would mean, say, a morning's opening, give or take, so Dr. Donia here on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While Mr. Ackerman thinks about it, Mr. de Roux will have the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just say that it depends on the material that's provided between now and then, with respect not just to Dr. Donia, but some of these other witnesses they have not provided the material on. Let me just say one thing before we start hearing it again from the Prosecutor: It's true, Your Honour, that I have signed receipts saying that I received certain documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to come to that. Again, that's a major -- anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I will not represent to you in writing, orally, or otherwise that I don't have a document when I do, in fact, have it. Now, many of the receipts -- the indexes that came with the receipts that I signed, the documents that were represented to be in that shipment were not there, and I have advised them of that on most of those occasions. The issue is not whether I received them or not but whether I have them. When I tell you I don't have them, I don't have them. And I can't do anything until I do have them. So the simple solution to that is that they give them to me again, because I just don't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You understand that the position that I have to take in that regard is to disagree completely with you in saying what's important is not whether I have received them; what's important is whether I have them. That's your problem. What concerns the Tribunal is whether they have been delivered to you. I can appeal to the Prosecution -- if you don't have them, I can ask Ms. Korner, please hand them over as quickly as you can, and I'm sure that Ms. Korner will come along. But don't tell me not having received them and not having them equals the same thing. It doesn't. It's not the same thing. And you, as an experienced lawyer, you know what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at my motions, you will see that I do not claim that I didn't receive them. What I claim is that I don't have them. And I don't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But that is a problem that can be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that. It's simple for that problem to be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Ackerman, that I, as a Judge, have been trained and also have and bound to put everything in a legal compartment. So if I have to put everything in a legal compartment, the way I have to approach it is if you don't have them, that may be a practical problem which can be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you tell me I don't have them because I have not received them, that becomes a problem for the Tribunal. If you don't tell me that, or rather you tell me not having received them and not having them is the same thing, or -- that's not the case. I mean, it no longer remains my problem. Again, I appeal to Ms. Korner. Please tell Ms. Korner what you require, and I am sure that you will -- she will make them available. And if necessary, I will postpone starting the trial until Wednesday if that is necessary for you to read these documents. I am prepared to meet you halfway. But don't present it to me as a problem, as a legal problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It becomes a legal problem to me if you tell me, "I don't have them because she never gave them to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no. Judge, there have been - I don't know - a hundred thousand of pages of documents supplied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, and you lost track of it. And I would have lost track, like I have done in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A document can be misfiled. It could be somewhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That can be solved. That is a practical problem, and I think there can be a practical solution to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, may I say this: That normally Mr. Ackerman writes to us and says he hasn't received the documents or whatever, and we do our best. It perhaps would have been more helpful if he had spoken to us rather than filing these motions. In fact, in some cases, Your Honour, we've provided the translations that he complains he hasn't had -- there are some, however, which are still awaiting translation. So that's certainly correct. It's the usual problem. Your Honour, we will resupply exceptionally today the documents that we do have translations of. I believe there are a number which are still awaiting translation into one or another language. But I'll go through them with him. But can I say, Your Honour, it's much more work than it sounds to extract these documents again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is it. I came to this Tribunal, and then suddenly learning -- it's the first time in my life that a couple of days before the trial is supposed to start, there are so many pending issues and so many complications. In the jurisdiction I come from, which is very similar to yours, everything is cooked and well cooked and nicely presented before it's eaten. Here we run the risk of going to table and -- having uncooked --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, having said that, the third witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We Maltese are like the French. We make of cooking and eating an art. So to us it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention the third witness on Your Honour's list, Witness 799?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me go to it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forgive me, I'm just trying to find -- yes. Your Honour, I'll deal with that with Mr. Ackerman after Your Honour has risen. We are unable to identify at the moment, I have to tell you, from what he's put in there, what documents he's referring to, because no ERN numbers have been given. Those are the numbers at the bottom. He will be the third witness and arrangements are in train because, as Your Honour may or may not know, the Victim and Witness Service require quite a lot of advance notice for getting witnesses here and arranging their travel. So therefore, it's relatively important to know, with that third witness, whether Mr. Ackerman is -- will maintain that he can't deal with him. He's coming from quite a long way away as well, and his travel is, again, quite expensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm going to do, Ms. Korner - and actually I was coming to this later on with regard to the motions filed by Mr. Ackerman - it was my intention to decide here and now, today, the motion dealing with Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was also my intention to give the Prosecution until tomorrow afternoon, end of business day tomorrow afternoon, to file a reply with regard to the other four motions, unless you want to reply to them in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if that is the case, we will come to them towards the end of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish what I had on my agenda, and we will come to them and then they will be decided between today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is, of course, because we don't know with that particular witness what these documents are, because the numbering means nothing to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman is going to tell you. I saw him nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've got them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, there is a practical solution to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may well be we will have to ask Your Honour to rise again because we have to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm here at your disposal. I have no dates or no arrangement or commitments. Mr. de Roux, sorry for keeping you too long waiting to make your intervention. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall be very brief. I should like to come back to the question of the witness, the expert who is going to give us a political opinion of political matters. There are other experts who are equally competent as this distinguished professor to discuss the affairs of the Balkans and to have an opinion as to what happened in this tragic affair. Therefore, the opinion of Professor Donia is certainly interesting but not that essential. That being so, let us go back to the position of the Defence. A moment ago, you used a culinary example that I share: The cooking has not been done and we are getting ready to eat raw. So I don't see any problem personally for Mr. Donia to come and testify if that would please the Prosecution. What I am saying simply is two things. If Mr. Donia testifies on Monday, I would like the Prosecution to withdraw this packet of documents, which is testimony already made by Mr. Donia. This is of secondary interest in my opinion. So if the Prosecution would be kind enough to withdraw these documents, we would not have to debate these very interesting historical documents of Mr. Donia by Monday, and then we would ask for time to be able to cross-examine Mr. Donia, because we can't do it immediately. After all, this is something for specialists, and the Defence reserves the right to call other experts, the Donias of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence, to come and testify on the same events from a different outlook. So if the Prosecution agrees to withdraw the object of this debate, these new documents which we do not have time to familiarise ourselves with, then the Defence of General Talic would be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I will withdraw them on the spot. I'm just waiting for Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to tell you the truth, Ms. Korner, I had a big temptation to suggest it to you, but I hesitated, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it is without doubt the most wonderful suggestion I've heard in the two years, three months, and ten days that I've been on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose Mr. Ackerman is going to insist on their being exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been here four years, in one role or another, at this Tribunal, and I knew -- I expected the day would come when I would step through the looking glass and be in a totally different dimension, and I think it just happened. These documents aren't supplied as proposed exhibits. Their purpose is not that they be exhibits in the case and become part of the record of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I was looking at them, even though I hadn't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Their purpose is that the Prosecution must give us prior statements of witnesses so that we can use them to prepare our cross-examination of the witnesses. The Prosecution never intended that they become exhibits in the case. So withdrawing them is of no -- makes no sense. I understand Ms. Korner is delighted to withdraw them because she just as soon we didn't read them and use them to cross-examine her witness, but she has to supply them. It's required by the Rules. That doesn't mean they are here as exhibits. None of this is here as exhibits. It's here to assist us in preparing cross-examination, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if there is no insistence on the Defence for the presence in the records of the case, we can live without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is, on behalf of this defendant, that any prior statement of any witness they are going to call needs to be provided. That's what the Rules require, and I insist on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's perhaps a sign of the difference between the two systems, which doesn't obviously often materialise in such an obvious way. Clearly, they are not intended as exhibits. They are supplied as previous testimony of a witness, and they are there for the Defence to use, if they so wish to, for the purposes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So they will remain there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are not an exhibit; they never were. They were supplied, as I said, because it's previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can safely move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, so Your Honour is going to rule later today, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. You think I am going to leave this pending? No way. With regard to Rule 92 bis statements, I stated -- one moment. Yes. I stated that there is an outstanding motion from General Talic that will be decided in due course. General Talic. Is there anything else pending under Rule 92 bis statements? In other words, you had presented a list under 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last time when we had the Pre-Trial Conference, you had stated that, more or less, you had 70 to 75 witnesses with regard to whom you intended to use 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have not gone back and added them up, but I think it's something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Something like that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it stand as it was or are there any changes or are there any additional --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there are, Your Honour. What our proposal was, was that we should deal with them municipality by municipality, but there is a motion by Mr. Ackerman objecting to the method, and it seems to me that has to be decided first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is again something -- you see, I am more or less in the same position than you are, even worse, because you filed it, so you came to know it -- know about it much --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just bringing it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution knew about it and it only arrives -- this is what you referred to before, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no. I just filed that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know about the prior motion, but you asked about 92 bis and I just wanted to bring you up to date because I know you don't have that yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was a motion put in by Mr. Ackerman on the 13th of December. It's listed in our -- attached to our agenda, which we responded to. We have had no ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is pending; yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as I know, neither counsel for General Talic has put in a motion about the 92 bis. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I said General Talic. Actually, I had intended Mr. Brdjanin. That's where he -- where, actually, what is being contested is not just one but all on the basis that the presiding officer walked out when -- so that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the principle, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That is what is going to be decided. I'm sorry if I referred to it as being General Talic's. It's Mr. Brdjanin's. But apart from that, there is nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But Your Honour, it's one of the many things that needs decision-making because we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, not that, it's whether or not because we have -- we can apply to Your Honour, in the teeth of Defence objections, to allow us to read these statements. It's Your Honour's decision, the Chamber's decision. So what we intend to do today was supply Your Honour with copies of the statements for the Banja Luka municipality that we wished to adduce under that rule, unless there is an objection to it, but it doesn't seem to me Your Honour can make a ruling at whatever stage you do and we'd ask that it's before -- in enough time to warn the witnesses and bring them here, if necessary, without reading what's in the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that -- disclosure has -- there are no problems pending with regard to disclosure, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All witness statements have been disclosed. I'm reminded - I checked again in the adjournment - all witness statements have been disclosed and translations that we are intending to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what is most important for the Tribunal to know. As regards the Tribunal itself, I would be quite satisfied to have them on a rolling basis, municipality by municipality. It would help me having it that way rather than all together - I think you understand what I mean - because we will have to live the trial day by day or municipality by municipality in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just, while I'm on my feet, raise one matter not so much -- but in connection with motions? Your Honour has said that there will be a ruling on the two outstanding motions that General Talic has in respect of the indictment, not the appeal. It's obviously vital, for the Prosecution's purposes, to know before we open the case whether the indictment is as it is, and -- or whether it's going to be amended again. The denial -- if the motions are denied, of course, General Talic has the right to appeal, and we could go on like this forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But you -- I think my message was quite clear in the beginning of today's hearing. There is an appeal pending, which I have had indication - although I can only speak for myself and for my Chamber and not for the Appeals Chamber - but the indication is that you don't have to worry about starting a trial without the appeal having been decided, because the appeal will in all probability be decided before the trial starts. And of course, how the trial starts depends on how the appeal will be decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an application for leave, Your Honour, not an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, an application for leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's still a question of the motions that are before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, there is a common terrain between the two motions outstanding before this Chamber and the substance of the grounds brought forward in the motion of General Talic for leave to appeal. So basically, I think I could leave it at that for the time being. I'm fully aware of what is involved and what's not, and I fully appreciate what your position is and what their position is. This is why I'm telling you, if the trial starts Monday, and there is -- I can assure you there is no way you can come here, you are going to come here Monday still in the clouds, as far as these two motions are concerned, or as far as the General Talic's motion for leave to appeal is concerned. That's definitely -- I've been trying to clear up the terrain before even today's sitting commenced. The other -- the only problem remaining is whether you wanted to start Monday or whether you wanted to start Wednesday. Please don't leave it hanging, Mr. Ackerman. Do tell me at some point in time what your preference is, and also Mr. Pitron and Mr. de Roux, whether you prefer to start Wednesday rather than Monday. But do tell me towards the end of the sitting. Next item on my agenda was the problem that was raised during the previous sitting regarding the admission of transcripts from other cases before the Tribunal. During the previous conference, Pre-Trial Conference, I had drawn your attention to part of the decision of Judge Hunt of the 23rd of November whereby he had drawn a distinction between certain events and certain other matters. And I had suggested to keep a distinction between certain issues like the internationality of the conflict and other matters like the existence of the conflict. Counsel for General Talic had agreed more or less to this. Counsel for Brdjanin, Mr. Ackerman, had reserved asking for time. I wonder if you have some kind of response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I've lost track of the question, Your Honour. What is it you would like to know from me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, during the previous conference, Pre-Trial Conference, the Prosecution had indicated even before and during the Pre-Trial Conference that it intended to tender transcripts of evidence given in other cases before this Tribunal, obviously with regard to facts, and also with regard to decided -- I think perhaps you could indicate now to Mr. Ackerman what your intentions were at the time. Because these were matters that were raised before Judge Hunt during the some of the status conferences anyway, and Judge Hunt went into the matter in his decision, and he drew your attention to certain matters, saying please don't try to do this. Keep this distinct from the rest, concentrate on the camps, for example, but not on the internationality of the conflict, et cetera, et cetera. We brought this up during the last Pre-Trial Conference, and more or less I made the same appeal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have some difficulty, I'm afraid, rather than like Mr. Ackerman. The answer is in the adjudicated facts which Your Honour has got, we asked, for example, the Defence to admit the convictions in the Keraterm case by way of a plea of guilty and thereby accepting that Keraterm was a place where offences were committed, and so on and so forth. Nothing has been agreed, so we have to make an application to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That explains. I thought that you had advanced somewhere ahead in that direction. You haven't?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I was acting under the impression that you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it may be what we're talking about here is that the Prosecution at one point presented us with some transcripts of testimony in prior cases regarding the internationality of the conflict and suggested that those transcripts should be accepted and that the Prosecution not be required to bring witnesses to establish the internationality of the conflict. And to some extent, it makes sense that that prior testimony simply be the testimony upon which this Chamber can base its decision. The problem is, at least in one instance that I'm aware of, the only transcript that was provided was the direct examination of the witness, leaving out the cross-examination which, in my humble view, brought some of the witness's statements into question. So if it's going to be done, and it probably is, then the Prosecutor should be required to provide the Chamber not just with the direct examination, which is very favourable, of course, to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is definitely correct, Mr. Ackerman. But apart from that, there is another consideration which you seem to be missing, both of you. During the last Pre-Trial Conference, in regard to this particular point that we are discussing now, and precisely with regard to the internationality of the conflict, I had drawn your attention to what Judge Hunt had stated in the 23rd November judgement decision; namely, that there is no point in asking on the part of the Prosecution to have the internationality of the conflict issue presented by way of an adjudicated fact while other things could be presented as adjudicated fact. And Judge Hunt had also suggested to the Prosecution to concentrate more on the camps. Now, there is a particular part of the 23rd -- if you give me the copy of the judgement of the 23rd, I will refer you precisely --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll have a look. I haven't got it with me at the moment, but I'll have a look. He wanted us to try and reach -- I do recall, Your Honour, roughly. He was asking us to try and reach some agreement, for example, that Omarska was set up, and so on and so forth. Your Honour, we have served, Your Honour will see, I've forgotten how many agreed facts there are, covering a wide variety of topics. As I've said to Your Honour, and I can give Your Honour the correspondence from the Defence, almost nothing is agreed. It is highly disappointing, may I say, that we should have to in one sense take up valuable court time proving matters about which there really should be no issue and which have no, as it were, direct impact on the Defence case in the sense that in most of these things, they are not suggested defendants personally took part. And it is not very helpful to say, in my view, for the management of a case, You brought these charges against the defendants, the accused; you must prove them; and we will not admit anything, other than the most innocuous of facts relating to the biography of the accused. And may I say, it isn't even apparently agreed that General Talic took command of the 1st Krajina Corps in March, or whenever it was, of 1992. It seems to me wholly incredible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe somewhere the document -- and not the 23rd November, but basically -- I don't have the document here, but I came across it and that's why I mentioned it the last time. You will find it somewhere. My predecessor excluded the possibility of having transcripts from other cases filed, presented on the internationality of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've added to -- since we had this discussion and since we gave the original binders to the Defence, we have added to the documents within the international armed conflict aspect, other documents have come to light which we say demonstrate clearly that by the definition of what is an international armed conflict, in the Talic case, the evidence is there. I'm sorry that, again, time should be taken in a trial worrying about whether or not the conflict was an international one when, as I say, it has already been decided in not just one but at least two cases in this Tribunal. And it is, as I say, somewhat unfortunate that time should be taken up proving that element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, length of the trial. We discussed this somewhat last time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm really somewhat weary of constantly being accused by the Prosecution of making it difficult for the trial to be held. I don't have that feeling. One point and one point alone: Madam Prosecutor claims that I was refusing to acknowledge -- that I would not acknowledge what was clear, that General Momir Talic was the commander of the 5th Corps of the JNA. I would like to make it clear that the question that she asked me, on 493 in her document of 29 December 2001, [In English] "Mr. Momir Talic was appointed commander of the JNA 5th Corps which..." 5th Corps, yes, but you continue -- but you continue, and you say, "...which on 19th May, 1992, was redesignated of the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of the VRS." No. So I can't agree with the 943 [sic] proposition you made. I am ready to accept some things, but not everything. [Interpretation] That's all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron just raised an issue that I ran into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. over and over. Ms. Korner didn't put facts in. She put in a fact which I could easily agree with, but then the next sentence was a conclusion based upon that fact which I can't agree with. And we're going to work all this out, Judge. But as I told you before, until I can read everything, I can't make these kind of decisions. But a lot of these things are going to get taken care of in agreements between the Prosecutor and the Defence, I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eventually, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just not going to happen today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see that, but I also anticipate what you're saying. Again, we all anticipate this trial to be a long one. Do you think there is reason for the Tribunal to believe or think that the trial will be longer than what was stated during the last Pre-Trial Conference, or shorter, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I said between 12 and 15 months, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't actually hear what the Defence said. That was my best guess, but it really depends on -- one of the things is when we are sitting. It appears that that the Defence and the Prosecution have two different court schedules, because the schedule that I've seen shows us sitting straight through, say, for a couple of days, and which I hope is right because may I say, Your Honour, five hours a day is not a lot of time with translation and breaks. That's the difficulty. I'm not even sure it's five hours. I think it's less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's less. It is actually from 9.00 until a quarter to 2.00 I think, yes. Something like that with breaks, et cetera. Anyway, we will have to talk about that, and we will have to plan as we go along as well. Okay, and I will be coming to some fundamental points which will have a bearing on how the trial will progress and how long it will take or last. There were two very important matters that were raised during the last previous conference that I am going to refer you to. In that regard, the authenticity of documents and also signatures. On behalf of defendant Brdjanin, there was a submission that documents purporting to be emanating from ARK, containing his alleged signature, with very few exceptions - that's the way you put it last time - were not signed or approved by him, nor issued with his permission. On that occasion, Ms. Korner had asked for clarification, and you had clarified, Mr. Ackerman, that it was your contention that the purported signature on a large number of these documents -- purported signature of your client was actually not his. You had promised on that occasion to provide the OTP with a list identifying the documents where you were alleging that your client's signature was not an authentic one. Has that been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The letter was sent out, and the Prosecution has been provided of a list of each of those documents that is a genuine signature of Brdjanin. I'm trying to find the date. I think I even have the receipt. But in any event, it has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, you're quite right. Mr. Ackerman provided me a copy. Again, I mentioned this, and said we hadn't had it, so it must have been very recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was faxed to Ms. Korner yesterday at 18.20 Greenwich mean time and it took 34 seconds for it to be transmitted, and she should have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who said that, "The righteous man sins seven times a day"? We all commit the same sins, I see, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's so nice to have her say, "I didn't receive it."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will accept that it's perfectly possible that if it was only faxed yesterday I haven't received it. Your Honour, I mention in connection with that something that happened last time. I said in that event, I would -- we would wish to seek handwriting samples from the accused, and that I appreciated that Mr. Ackerman couldn't answer straight away because he would have to take instructions. Mr. Ackerman answered straight away, without having taken instructions. Now, the only reason I raise it because the person who is going to suffer from a failure to provide handwriting specimens, if asked, is not Mr. Ackerman but his client, because it is to his client, if he gives evidence, that it will be put he declined to give those handwriting samples because he knew full well that they would show by comparison that these documents did have his handwriting. And so I raise it now. I think there is a difference between our systems there. Effectively, counsel don't act without instructions in my system, and it may be in Your Honour's as well. Therefore, I think it only right that Mr. Brdjanin should hear the point that is being made. The second matter is handwriting is now apparently in dispute in General Talic's quarter. In the response to the agreed facts, it was disputed that some unidentified documents bore -- which appeared to have his signature, is his signature. Again, we have written asking for those documents to be identified, and that hasn't happened, unless there has been a fax yesterday which I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Two things. Number one, the handwriting exemplars will not be given. Number 2, there is a very comprehensive decision with regard to handwriting exemplars which was issued by the Trial Chamber in Celebici. We had, as I recall, at least a full day's argument, full briefing and a very comprehensive decision. That decision takes the position that handwriting exemplars are like statements of witnesses, that they can represent -- that the witness is entitled to remain silent and not give statements, also entitled not to give handwriting exemplars, and in all those cases that involve the witness's right to remain silent, that it is absolutely improper and totally improper for the Prosecution to comment on his right to remain silent and his silence or to comment upon his failure to give handwriting exemplars. So not only is the Prosecutor not going to get them, but I suggest that it's improper for her to comment to this Chamber that that somehow is evidence of guilt on his part. It's just that we are not going to give them, and we have a right not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner comes from a jurisdiction where that practice has changed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know it has changed but I don't think it's changed in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's for me to decide later on. It's a question of how legal it is and how correct it is to draw inferences. But again, I would rather prefer that at the present moment -- first of all, your client has every right to remain silent; there is no question about it. So let's leave it at that. You have made a statement on his behalf, that he is not going to make available specimens of his handwriting, and the matter stops there for the time being. That will be pleasures yet to come in due course, but at this point in time, we are not going to discuss it any further and the matter is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, if you heard me trying to pre-empt your right to make a decision on that, I was not doing that. I was telling you what the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. Mr. Pitron, I understood that you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It seems to me that my last statement was clear and that you understood it well. I can repeat it, but I don't think that will be necessary regarding this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I'd like a response from Mr. Pitron. Am I going to be provided with numbers of the documents on which they say the handwriting of General Talic is in dispute? And equally, I will make the same request, for whatever it's worth, that the General provide us with samples of his handwriting, if it's going to be a matter of dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. And while you are preparing to answer those two queries, may I remind you, Mr. Pitron, that during the previous conference, you had made a statement challenging the authenticity of a number of documents, without specifying them, but you had also stated that the -- there are documents that you were prepared -- or your client was prepared to accept coming from the 1st Krajina Corps collection, and you promised to give an indication to the Prosecution as to which documents from the 1st Krajina Corps collection you were prepared to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be useful to recall my position, which will respond to the request of Ms. Korner. There are three types of documents. The first are those bearing the signature of General Talic. There is no reason for me, a priori, to contest the authenticity of those documents. I repeat that they are very numerous. If, in the course of the proceedings, it should appear to me that one of them is false, that the signature of the General is false, I would let it be known. I will provide the necessary proof for this, and the Court will judge. Today, I am not aware of documents bearing General Talic's signature with an imitated signature or a falsified one. A second type of documents are those documents carrying the words "signed for" or "za" in Serbo-Croatian. I frequently don't know the signature that is on those documents. It is quite clear if those documents were signed on behalf of General Talic, I would not know them, and therefore, I am expressing my reservation regarding the possibility of confronting General Talic with those documents as coming under his responsibility. There is a third type of document, and those are the ones that are attributed to General Talic and which strictly do not contain any element of identification. There may be just a header on the document, a seal or a signature. I do not have to prove that those documents come from General Talic or do not come from General Talic. It is up to the Prosecution to show if they really come from General Talic. It's not my problem. It's theirs. On these -- on the basis of these -- this differentiation, I do not see why I should provide the Prosecution with any document at all, if I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think just close on this and we'll have to make a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour wants to hear from me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite wrong. It is up to the Defence. We have submitted an exhibit list in which we have set out all the exhibits we intend to produce. If the Defence do not let us know that these documents, the admissibility of that is disputed or the signature is disputed, they go in as accepted documents. It is quite impossible for us to go from one day to the next and suddenly Mr. Pitron announces that General Talic, faced with a document, or a witness, faced with a document that apparently bears his signature, is in fact disputed. Your Honour, we served a witness list and we made a request to both counsel -- not, witness, I'm sorry, exhibit list - to let us know which documents are in dispute. I understand that many of the documents - and I think it was made clear - were in dispute. It is not right that the Defence can say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, to be precise, one of the things that emerged from the last Pre-Trial Conference, Mr. Pitron, was that you were actually questioning the authenticity of all documents. This is how it started. And in actual fact, at that point in time, we had a cross debate asking sort of, "What's the situation then? Do I have to prove the authenticity of each document?" And I told you, Ms. Korner, that may well be a problem which you are prepared for now, and you should know, as an experienced Prosecutor, how to deal with it, and you should have whoever needs to confirm the authenticity of the document ready to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm calling -- in connection with that, the second witness after Dr. Donia will be the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is as a result -- that is something that came up. Then Mr. Pitron realised, in my opinion, the consequences of what he had stated, and he said, of course, what he is contesting is the authenticity of those documents that purport to be attributed to General Talic when, in actual fact, on the face of them, there is nothing to show that they are attributable to General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also said, "There are some documents which, of course, we do not dispute the authenticity of." And he -- and he made a specific reference to some documents coming from the 1st Krajina Corps collection. What that means, don't ask me. I don't know. I will learn in due course what the 1st Krajina Corps collection means. But he promised -- you promised, Mr. Pitron, to give an indication to the Prosecution which documents you were not contesting, the consequence being that all the rest was being contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me break here, give you time to think about this, and we will convene in a quarter of an hour's time. In the meantime, we can have a coffee. --- Break taken at 6.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue with this understanding, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because of -- thank you for reminding me. Yes, good evening. Let's continue with this understanding, that because of arrangements, interpretation and all that, we have to stop at 7.00. And then what happens after that, I will tell you later. Because of the fact that we are stopping at 7.00, I am going to postpone certain matters for the time being. Finish off with Mr. Pitron first, listen to what he has to say; then deal very briefly with the five motions of Mr. Ackerman now, since you are prepared to provide the Tribunal with an oral response. That's what I understood. Okay? And then we'll take it up from there. So Mr. Pitron, please. I don't need to remind you what you are supposed to...

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that was asked by the Prosecutor is whether I am going to provide her with a list of witnesses that I am contesting. I have a simple answer. I will, of course, do that on the basis of the documents that I received today, that is the list of facts that she is going to submit to the parties, to the Tribunal, as part of the trial which is about to begin. And so I learned about that list today. This requires work with my collaborators who speak Serbo-Croat, because I am speaking about the documents in Serbo-Croat. I am going to verify them immediately, those that are on the list, and those that I contest will be indicated to her on the basis, however, of the three-fold definition which I provided a little while ago which, in my opinion, goes a long way in reducing any uncertainties about the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at total cross-purposes, I don't know whether it's deliberate or not or because it's late, what Mr. Pitron is referring to is we have given the Defence today a list of the documents referred to in Dr. Donia's statement, the disclosure numbers. What I am talking about is the schedule of all the exhibits in the case which the Defence have had since we served the Rule 65 documents. I want to know what -- if it's the greater, what they are prepared to admit. In other words, whichever is -- I'm sorry -- whichever is the lesser, i.e. which do they dispute or which do they admit? I refer again to handwriting. It is no good Mr. Pitron suddenly announcing that a particular document that is going to be produced by a particular witness the next day, the handwriting is disputed. We are obviously, if we are told handwriting is disputed, going to try and carry out analysis of some kind. In his response to the adjudicated facts, under (h), documents in support of an international armed conflict -- and it may assist if I give Your Honour a copy of this. It was in French originally, and we've had it translated. And I'm sure Mr. Pitron can give you a copy of the original if there's a dispute about the translation. But if Your Honour turns to the last page, under (h), documents in support of an international armed conflict, the documents referred to by the Prosecutor in Part 9 of her pretrial brief are not agreed. A whole series of documents come from unknown sources. The documents -- and this is the particular paragraph -- the documents which according to the Prosecutor are signed by General Talic do not bear his signature. Now, unless I'm misreading it, that is an avowal that documents, particularly within this context and many of the documents that are being adduced in support of an international armed conflict, are military in source, do not bear his signature. Now, is that saying that documents which on the face of it are not signed for General Talic or on his behalf but actually have his signature, it is disputed that that is his signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that particular paragraph and sentence reads as follows: "The documents which, according to the Prosecutor are signed by General Talic, do not bear his signature." So basically, we are only referring here to those documents which, according to you, are signed by General Talic. Those are the only -- not documents which are made attributable to him because someone else signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I read it as it is written and I understand it as it is written, and as it is written, we are only talking of those documents which, according to you, are signed by General Talic. He is saying, "They do not bear my signature." That's where the matter starts and ends, as far as I'm concerned. So he is not distinguishing between some and more of those documents, which according to you are signed by him. He's saying, "All those documents which according to you are signed by me, do not bear my signature." This is how it reads. And this is how I have to take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right, Your Honour, and all I've asked for -- I wrote a letter saying, "Can we have the numbers of the documents to which you refer?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can say, "You should know because you know which documents you are saying are signed by me."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thousands, literally, thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is contesting them all. This is how I read it. He is telling you - and this is what his attitude was last time, if you recall - he is telling you here, "Documents which you say are signed by me are not signed by me."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but that's what I mean, Your Honour. It isn't clear, I'm sorry. It may just be me and it may be because it's late. Is he saying simply the documents that we've adduced in support of an international armed conflict or all the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. We are referring -- this is inserted in a numbered or lettered paragraph in his document, namely, documents in support of an international armed conflict. I do not have that sentence generally applicable to the whole documentation, that we are talking of documents which you are presenting in that context and which he is contesting only on the basis that what you allege to be his signature is not his signature. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, because we -- can I -- may I finish, Your Honour, please? The difficulty is if we don't get a response to our letters, I have to raise all these matters in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just be told, in open court so that I understand, it is only the documents inserted in the section international armed conflict and referred to in our pre-trial brief that are the subject of dispute? That where his signature on the face of the document appears to be his signature, that is disputed? That's all I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pitron, the ball is in your court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must be tired, Your Honour, but I don't see what the problem is. I have replied with precision. I don't have before me the document that I wrote, but listening to you rereading it, I responded to the request of the Prosecutor, H-132, and I said, documents relating to that paragraph [In English] international armed conflict [Interpretation] that I am contesting the signature under the conditions that I have specified. How can I put things differently? What is not clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask what is the difficulty in giving us the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I, as a Defence counsel, wouldn't give you the numbers either. I would tell you, "Listen, you know which documents you are going to present in support of an international armed conflict. All those documents that -- within that context that you are saying were signed by me were not signed by me." Full stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that matters are different in Your Honour's jurisdiction, but beyond me, I cannot see why common courtesy alone doesn't -- stops Mr. Pitron from giving me the numbers of the documents. It's nothing to do with defence or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably -- not probably, you are definitely right, but he probably has to go through tonnes and tonnes and tonnes or piles of papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, so do we. This is suddenly sprung on us at the last moment. Up until now, in the countless Status Conferences that we've had, not once was it suggested by anybody that we were going to have to be dealing with handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But everyone carries the responsibilities of his or her actions. So basically, if this is the way that he has chosen to follow, then obviously there are consequences to that. Your life may be made a little more difficult. Surely you cannot say that he is not telling you what he means. He is telling you here, "I mean all these documents." Full stop. It could have been -- it might give rise to problems later on. I'm quite aware of that. Because there may be documents which are used for this context -- in this context but also in other contexts and, in other words, they are not contested in one context and contested in another, but it's a question I wouldn't like to say much more about it. I mean, everyone carries the consequences of his actions. I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. It may not be that they are aware of the consequences of the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's not -- listen, I think I've said enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honour, all I want to ensure then -- and I had my answer, as Your Honour says, the handwriting is the subject of dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, definitely. So now, let's take these one by one. Let's start with the first motion by Mr. Ackerman on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin. In this case, I can mention the name of the witness, Robert Donia. The motion is for the testimony of Mr. Robert Donia to be delayed for a minimum of 30 days or not later than 21st of February, 2002. More or less, we have tackled bits and pieces of it, I would say even the substance of it, in conjunction also with the response of the Defence for General Talic and also in the context of your motion. So is there anything that you would like to add in regard to this particular motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Simply, as Your Honour rightly says, we've discussed this. My application would be that the case be put back until Wednesday to give the Defence what Your Honour may consider to be sufficient time to go through the previous material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, would you like to add anything in regard to your motion, taking into consideration what has been stated throughout by Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we have made serious efforts to deal with the problems here today, Your Honour, and I am at least somewhat satisfied that we are making progress in that regard as long as -- as long as the Chamber is prepared to give me the time that is necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber will give you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- be prepared to cross-examine, then I'm happy. That's what I'm really talking about in all these motions, is the necessity of being prepared to cross-examine. Maybe I can make the job easier for you, Judge, if I just say this: It seems to me that with regard to the translation problems, that with these Banja Luka witnesses and the documents that have not yet been provided, that there ought to be some way to prioritise the translation process so that those get done rather immediately, even if we just sort of suspend the rules of the Tribunal for a little while and have them done unofficially rather than by the Tribunal's staff so that the official ones can come later. I just need to know what some of these documents say before I can be convinced that I am ready to prepare myself to cross-examine the witness. And I think probably waiting until Wednesday is going to help, but it's only going to help if the Prosecutor can somehow undertake to get into my hands those documents that have yet to be translated, especially - most especially - the ones that have been provided to me only in B/C/S and have not been translated into English. It just makes it impossible for me to prepare a cross-examination because there may be something lying there that changes the whole aspect of the cross. And so I think if we were to wait until Wednesday, and if those documents could be provided as quickly as possible on a priority basis, then I suspect most of the reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These documents relate to Donia's evidence, or not? Because I understood throughout that those documents referred to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've moved on to the next lot. The documents, there are extra documents. I'm more or less confident that they will be translated by Friday. So the Donia ones will be ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with the subsequent witnesses, if we can just prioritise that process and get those done as quickly as possible, we can move forward. And if it could be the mission at this point that the witnesses that are next in line, that the untranslated documents with regard to those witnesses get the highest priority. It makes no sense for the people that are doing the translation to be working on a witness we're going to call ten months from now when we are all concerned about a witness we are going to call next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be wise to prioritise, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we do that, I think we can solve a lot of problems. If we don't do that, I can see that this is just going to be a continuing, continuing problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be a big headache. I would suggest --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can tell, Your Honour, they are already at the top of the priority list. Some of the documents, if I take the next motion as it has been numbered, which relates to Witness 764, that's D7668 on the top, there's the -- you see paragraph 5 of that particular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first document referred to has already been disclosed, but we'll give, as I say, a "once in a lifetime" opportunity and repeat the disclosure, there is a translation of that. The following series of numbers to the words "and no Serbian translation," these were all thrown up by the witness searches. They have been in for translation but only went in in December because that's when the search actually threw them up. They, in fact, relate to an arrest of the witness during the war in Bosnia. What we can do is we can provide summaries, but it does just occur to me, of course, that Mr. Ackerman does have a certain advantage in that his co-counsel, of course, speaks the language, is a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, of course, Mr. Ackerman has referred to previous case law of the Tribunal in other matters, not on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we're doing the best we can, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's a problem, and we have to live with it. But we have to find a solution also. And what is important is what Mr. Ackerman stated, and that is there is room for prioritising, and I would suggest we do it municipality by municipality. I think that's where the -- where you ought or your office ought, in conjunction with the translations. And obviously, it has to be a concerted effort. But the direction on the part of your office should be, for the time being, concentrate on what needs to be translated municipality by municipality as planned. You know, it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the way, when we have sent in requests to the translation unit. I may say I'm fully in favour of Mr. Ackerman's suggestion, and that is that we use, I'm afraid, unauthorised translations. Only if there is a real dispute about the nature of the translation does it go in for revision. But I know that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can live with that. I have nothing against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the department that runs the translation does have severe reservations about that, and I think there will be a problem. With respect, I think it's something that perhaps Your Honours and the translation unit will have to sort out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's something that has cropped up already in proceedings of this case and also in others, and also something that we discussed, Judges, amongst ourselves recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, our feeling is much the same, that we should now, for expediency's sake, adopt the method that translation is done by a not-fully-qualified member of the language staff. Only if there is an argument as to the correctness of the translation will it go in for revision. We can, if it helps, Mr. Ackerman -- and as I say, when we went through these motions, we discovered that, according to our records, we've disclosed a lot of these, and we can redisclose them with translation. The only one, as I said, is the one in relation to the Witness 7.99, which is in motion D7672. And Mr. Ackerman I think will write out the relevant ERN numbers for us, and we will go and check them overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That, he promised to give in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that in mind, from what I understand, Mr. Ackerman is not pursuing those motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's up to Mr. Ackerman to -- I mean, the way I was trying to lead the debate was precisely towards that direction. But of course, there are ifs and buts. And one if and but is your promise to have translations of certain documents ready by Friday, and that is crucial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we are all lawyers here, and you know, I mean, it's...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in normal circumstances, it wouldn't cause so much of a problem. But I don't know whether Your Honour has had a chance to have any discussions with the Victims and Witness Units. It's a complicated procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I know what the problems are, and it terrifies me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why it's important to know before we bring them here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what ought to be done is this: I mean, having met you twice already here, I have more or less the conviction now that I am dealing with reliable professionals. I don't doubt your words for a minute, and I don't doubt your good intentions and the humungous effort that you are all making in order to get things going. I realise you all have difficulties, and please do know that I am full of understanding. I know that the problems are enormous, not just on your side but also on your side, and in certain areas, your problems are bigger than yours because you always have, to an extent, an advantage in certain areas, especially when it comes to possession of documents. What I was going to suggest is this: That I give, on the understanding that the translation of Mr. Donia's report annexed to your motion will be available in B/C/S not later than Friday, I make an order today rejecting Mr. Ackerman's request for a delay in having him brought here as a witness when we start next week, with the reservation that this decision will be automatically reversed if the translation is not in place on Friday. That's number one. Number two, there is always the understanding - and I'm making myself clear - that this, of course, is not intended to prejudice in any way the rights of the defendants to a fair hearing, to be given every opportunity to be prepared for cross-examination. That will be dealt as we go along. I will be in a position, together with my colleagues who will be joining me at the time, to be able to make an assessment, a general assessment, as to whether we think Mr. Ackerman, for example, or Mr. Pitron, should be in a position to make the cross-examination or not. If we feel that it's a case of giving further time, we will give it. If it's the case of saying, "No, maximum, you have until tomorrow morning, and start your cross-examination," we will start the following morning. So this is more or less the plan that I have. With regard to the other motions, although there is an innate urgency to them as well because we are talking about witnesses that you have listed amongst the first to be produced, I see that there are two practical problems. One is your availability to provide Mr. Ackerman with documents that he would like to have, not necessarily that has not been delivered, but that he has not got at the present moment and which he would like to have because he needs them, and I have your word that you will be doing your utmost to hand them over to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will hand over what we've already disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there is the question of translations again here, but I think, as I read you, that should be a matter of a short time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying that, Your Honour. I'm saying the translation of the Donia report, but I can't say that it will be a short time before we give -- we get translation of the others. I just can't say that. We are still dependent on the availability of language staff, qualified or unqualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think we will have to visit that position as we go along, fully aware that, as you rightfully pointed out, Mr. Ackerman is also assisted by someone learned in the B/C/S languages. I think that's the way we have to approach it at the present moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask? Your Honour is not intending therefore, as I suggested, to put the case back to Wednesday which at least makes it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's my intention to put the case back to Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is no major opposition, and I don't foresee Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any major opposition. My intention also is that Mr. Donia, I will decide today, now, in more or less in the way I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The others, I will decide -- I will convene another Pre-Trial Conference to finish off what the -- the few things that need to be concluded Monday morning. Hopefully, that will be a short hearing. And Wednesday, when we start the trial, there will be four oral decisions on the remaining four motions of Mr. Ackerman, unless by that time, because of the exchange of information and also the availability of documents that may have been made in the meantime, he opts for a withdrawal of one or more or all of those motions. So that's the way I suggest we go about it. I would like to hear Mr. Ackerman, however, if he's got anything to say about this, about my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think your suggestion is fine, Your Honour. I think it's probably going to work. It really depends on how rapidly we can get translations. Just -- I'll be very brief, but just as a matter of candour, it seems to me that we are struggling mightily here to try to, by fits and starts, get a trial going. I think we are really about two weeks away from being ready. I think almost all these problems would be solved if we waited another two weeks to start this trial. I don't think that is in the cards. I don't think anybody in Chambers and everywhere else wants to do that, but I can assure you that things would go a lot more smoothly, and a lot of these things that are vexing and major problems today would be gone two weeks from now and there would be a lot less problem. We are working rapidly. We've made a lot of progress since the last conference. We are really, I think, a couple of weeks away from being ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be wishful thinking, I think. Let's not go into the merits of whether two weeks would provide us with the right medicine and solve it all, a panacea. I presume the trial will start on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I presume that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm sure things will fall into place as we go along. You will also realise that we need to start, because if we prolong it further and further, we will have more motions and more problems, and we will never start. And then we will need a further two weeks and a further three weeks. That's how it will go. I mean, please do remember, Mr. Ackerman, you are older than I am but I have been a Judge for the past 25 years, and I know that in conducting this kind of orchestra, the important thing is to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell by looking at me that I'm older than you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I know that you are older than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
